claim: Linked selection (hover over the mesh, press L to select all connected faces; Shift+L to deselect the linked faces) can be scoped with the Delimit setting in the operator panel: setting Delimit to Seam limits the flood-fill to the area bounded by UV seams (edges marked via Ctrl+E > Mark Seam), so pressing L inside one seam-bounded region selects only that region rather than the whole connected mesh. The narration frames this as a fast way to select different named areas of a mesh according to a shared boundary property, and notes Delimit can be set to other properties as well (not enumerated in the transcript).
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript (narration only, no frames), [25:01]-[25:46]: 'the linked selection... you hover above the mesh and press L and all the connected faces will be selected... this mesh has some red marked edges, I selected these edges, and then I pressed CTRL+E and marked them as seam... If I now press L over here and down here in the operator panel, I set the delimit to seam that means the linked selection will be limited to the area of the seams... which can be a great tool to quickly select different areas according to different properties. You can see you can delimit this to other properties as well.'
rejected_alternative: Manually box-selecting or painting the boundary of a named mesh area by hand instead of flood-filling to an existing seam boundary with L + Delimit: Seam.
reason: This project's decision-transaction protocol already does targeted selection programmatically via select_region/select_by_ids; this is the interactive-GUI equivalent mental model (flood-fill bounded by a marked property) worth knowing when reasoning about how a human modeler would isolate a mesh region, though the project has not yet needed UV seams for this purpose specifically.

claim: To end up with 'everything except one part' of a mesh selected, select the (usually simpler) part you want deselected first, then press Ctrl+I to invert the selection -- rather than selecting everything (A) and then Shift+L-deselecting the unwanted part by hand.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript (narration only, no frames), [25:46]-[26:13]: 'Sometimes you wanna select everything of your mesh, except one certain part. So you could select everything, and then with SHIFT+L, for example, deselect what you want, but the more complex your mesh is, the harder this can be... sometimes the easier way is to do it the other way around. That means I select the area first, which I want to have deselected, and then simply press CTRL+I to invert the selection, now I have everything else selected.'
rejected_alternative: Select-all (A) then Shift+L-deselect the unwanted region by hand -- explicitly called out in the narration as getting harder the more complex the mesh is.
reason: A general selection-strategy rule worth applying whenever a large majority of a mesh needs to be selected around a small excluded region: isolate the small/simple side first and invert, instead of trying to manually exclude it from a full selection.

claim: Checker Deselect (Select menu, applied after selecting one full loop) deselects every Nth element in a repeating pattern along that loop, with adjustable select-count, deselect-count, and offset exposed in the operator panel -- e.g. to select only every second face of a loop and then extrude just those faces for an alternating raised/recessed pattern.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript (narration only, no frames), [25:59]-[26:36]: 'Sometimes it can be useful to select every second face of a loop for example. In order to achieve this, select one loop, then go to select and click on Checker Deselect, now down here, you can also check how many should be deselected or how many should be selected, and you can also change the offset. So, and then you can, for example, extrude this stuff and create some pretty interesting results.'
rejected_alternative: Manually clicking every second face of a loop one at a time instead of selecting the whole loop and running a pattern-deselect.
reason: A quick way to produce alternating extrude/inset patterns (grille, tread, paneling detail) on a loop without hand-picking individual faces -- relevant to any future hard-surface detailing pass this project does with repeating panel patterns.

claim: Selecting one face/edge/vertex, then Ctrl-clicking a second one, selects the shortest connected path between them (Select Shortest Path), with operator-panel options: Face Stepping (a direct/unconnected shortcut path rather than following mesh connectivity), Topology Distance (fewest possible steps), and Fill Region (fills the entire enclosed area between the two selected faces). Fill Region also has a direct shortcut -- Ctrl+Shift+click a second face -- without opening the operator panel at all.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript (narration only, no frames), [26:43]-[27:35]: 'If you select a face, edge, or vertex, then hold down CTRL and select another one, the shortest path will be selected. Then down here we have some additional features, like face stepping... topology distance, which tries to make the selection with as few steps as possible, and then we have fill a region, which fills the whole region between these two faces. Which by the way, you can also use directly using a shortcut by holding down CTRL+SHIFT, and then left click, select another face. This one is so cool, you can select this one, CTRL+SHIFT, this one, and the whole area will be selected.' The narration also notes the same panel's select/deselect spinner can be set to deselect every second face of the resulting path, echoing the Checker Deselect pattern.
rejected_alternative: Manually box-selecting or loop-selecting every face inside a bounded area one at a time instead of Ctrl+Shift-clicking the two boundary faces and letting Fill Region select the whole enclosed patch in one step.
reason: Directly useful for selecting an irregular bounded patch of faces on a complex mesh (e.g. a panel region between two landmarks) in one click instead of manual selection -- a capability this project's typed selection ops (select_region/select_by_ids) don't currently expose as a 'shortest path between two IDs' or 'fill enclosed region' primitive.

claim: Shift+G opens Select Similar, which selects every other element sharing a chosen property with the currently active selection. In Edge mode this includes Bevel (Weight), so selecting one bevel-weighted edge and running Select Similar > Bevel selects every other edge on the mesh carrying that same bevel weight. In Face/Vertex mode it includes Face Normal, with an adjustable Threshold in the operator panel so faces whose normals are close-but-not-exactly-equal can be swept in too. The same command works in Object Mode on a selected object, offering properties like Type (e.g. selecting all mesh objects in the scene).
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript (narration only, no frames), [28:21]-[29:16]: 'this edge has now selected, and if I press SHIFT+G, I can open up the select similar menu... in this case, bevel, then it will select all the other edges on this mesh with the same property... the face normal, then it will select all the other faces with the same normal, and down here in the operator panel, I can also change the threshold... By the way, in object mode, this works quite similar. Select an object, hit SHIFT+G... For example, I can click on type, then all mesh objects in the scene will be selected.'
rejected_alternative: Manually hunting through the mesh (or scene) by eye for every other edge/face/object that shares a given property instead of selecting one instance and letting Select Similar find the rest.
reason: Directly relevant to this project's standing bevel-weight policy: once one edge has been given a bevel weight, Select Similar > Bevel is a fast way to verify or extend which other edges on the same mesh carry that weight, rather than re-deriving the set by re-inspecting each edge.
